title: Thinking Through the Difficult Decision to Terminate a Team Member
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece offers leaders a structured way to reason through one of the hardest calls they face: whether to terminate a team member. It lays out four canonical reasons for termination — underperformance, bad judgment, misconduct or compliance violations, and culture disruption — and notes that most real cases don't cleanly fit just one of them, which is exactly what makes the decision so agonizing. The article's central heuristic is that when more than one of the four reasons applies simultaneously, even partially, that overlap should tip the scales toward termination. This gives leaders a decision rule rather than leaving them to weigh vague, competing considerations in the abstract.
points: The essay supplies a concrete decision heuristic — overlap of two or more of the four termination categories should tip the scales — rather than leaving the call purely to gut feel.
It explicitly names why the decision feels so hard: most real cases involve reasons that are individually insufficient but collectively compelling.
The four-category framework (underperformance, bad judgment, misconduct, culture disruption) gives leaders a shared vocabulary for discussing hard cases with peers or HR.
It frames termination decisions as a search for corroborating evidence across categories rather than a single smoking-gun justification.
quotes: Generally speaking, there are four primary reasons why a leader would consider terminating a team member: Underperformance, Bad judgment, Misconduct or compliance violation, Culture disruption.

What makes the decision to terminate so difficult is not only that most team members make a valuable contribution in other areas, but that typically none of the reasons for dismissal are so blatantly bad as to warrant an immediate call.
The premise is that any team member who exhibits more than one reason at the same time should likely be shown the door.
Any time more than one of the four critical reasons for termination exists, a leader should use this as a signal that the time has come to make the tough call.
Team members who give leaders multiple reasons for termination make the decision a bit more straightforward.
